question: What did you like most about this prompt?
answer: The 'This computer' section, especially 'What this computer doesn't have'. Exact tool versions and a named stand-in for the controller, touch, sound and second player meant I could test the risky parts instead of guessing. It also left the real decisions open: genre, camera, how much research and how much effort. And the links held up: the engine built and played the first time, and the hub harness ran as documented.

question: What was confusing?
answer: Four things. (1) 'Multiplayer ... as well as for the game on its own': the hub README says a game outside a session is simply not affected, which reads as single-player, but the brief's wording could also mean multiplayer must exist with no hub. I planned for both readings: hub ghost sessions plus local pass-the-pad play. (2) The About screen must show a Usage line that a later agent fills in, but the engine packs game text inside gzipped wasm, and nothing says where that line must stay editable. I guessed a plain-text JSON block in the page. (3) 'Leave out TASK.md's file and folder names' does not say whether fixed names like the exit interview file count. I left them all out and wrote 'your brief'. (4) 'python3 -m http.server 0 ... prints it' is only true on a terminal: read through a pipe the port line is buffered, and my harness script hung until its timeout, twice, before I found out why (the fix is -u).

question: What was the hardest thing to do?
answer: Turning Wii Fit into an original controller-first game. Its identity rests on a peripheral a DualSense does not have and on character designs I must not copy, so I had to separate what makes it distinctive (tiny movements, a blunt daily verdict, equipment with opinions, a calm clinical tone) from how it looks. The second hardest was writing for builders of unknown ability who cannot ask me anything. That is why I built the engine and tested the risky seams myself on real builds: the hub protocol, the Rust-to-JavaScript link, the controller stub, custom fonts, set switching and browser tick rates. Those tests changed the plan: for example, the browser runs far below real time at normal window sizes, so its tests must run at 320x180.

question: What would you change in this prompt?
answer: State plainly whether a game on its own needs multiplayer or just has to run. Say where in the HTML the Usage line must stay editable. Change the server example to 'python3 -u -m http.server 0 --bind 127.0.0.1'. Tell the planner which models and how much time the builders will have, so the plan's scope can fit them; without that I wrote a full-size plan with a cut order. Give a target length for the plan, since every builder rereads it on every turn. And say outright that a planner may clone and build the engine and should clean up afterwards; I assumed so, and removed my clones when done.
